title: Marc Elias' Legal Team Threatens Media With Lawsuit For Questioning Roy Cooper's Health
desc:
Marc Elias' Legal Team Threatens Media With Lawsuit For Questioning Roy Cooper's Health

Authored by Jonathan Turley via Jonathan Turley,

Marc Elias has long been at the center of controversial election tactics, including criminal investigations. If lawyers had to take an oath to first do no harm, the court-sanctioned Democratic lawyer would leave Hippocrates gobsmacked. Well, Elias is back and his legal team is threatening the media with what appears an entirely meritless defamation lawsuit on behalf of former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for the United States Senate.

This seems to be an effort to deter the media from raising the issue of the health of Cooper, who is 69 years old. Such health related issues have been much in the news for politicians ranging from former President Joe Biden to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.).

It is obviously a legitimate matter for media inquiry and the threat seems designed to deter others from raising the issue before the midterm elections. In typical Elias fashion, it is a smash-mouth approach that only generated national coverage of the issue - working against the interests of his client.

The North State Journal reported that it had asked the Cooper campaign if there were any health problems that might impede him from completing his term:

"North State Journal (NSJ) has previously emailed questions to the campaign eight times this year, and all but two went unanswered. The ninth time, NSJ received a cease-and-desist letter threatening legal action from the Elias Law Group.

The Journal reports on such stories as "the only statewide newspaper in North Carolina."

In a letter to make this "exceedingly simple and crystal clear to you," the lawyer for the Elias Law Group warned the Journal that any suggestion that Cooper is "'experiencing a neurological issue,' or that any health condition would prevent him from completing his term, is categorically false and defamatory."

While I have taught torts for 30 years, I must be missing the Elias Group's simple clarity on this issue. In demanding that the media "cease and desist," the Elias Group lays out the defamation law in North Carolina in making "false, defamatory statements of or concerning the plaintiff, which were published to a third person, causing injury to the plaintiff's reputation."

Notably, the Elias Group stated that "a publication that is obviously defamatory constitutes defamation per se." That specific assertion is challengeable if it is referring to the common-law per se categories. Such a publication can be defamation, but the per se categories are laid out as a matter of state law. (The letter goes on to make a more specific per se defamation claim).

The common law per se categories began as categories of slander where damages would be presumed in the same way as libel. The allegation would fall into one of the "per se" categories of defamation. Under the common law, these per se categories of defamation allow for presumed damages and include: (1) disparaging a person's professional character or standing; (2) alleging a person is unchaste; (3) alleging that a person has committed a criminal act or act of moral turpitude; (4) alleging a person has a sexual or loathsome disease; and (5) attacking a person's business or professional reputation.

North Carolina has a broad definition of defamation per se, including alleging that the person (1) has committed an infamous crime; (2) has an infectious disease; (3) imputes a person's trade or profession; or (4) otherwise tends to subject one to ridicule, contempt, or disgrace. That last category is obviously somewhat elastic.

The letter references a more specific basis for a per se category for "imputing insanity or impairment of mental faculties is libelous per se." Jarman v. Offutt, 239 N.C. 468, 472 (1954). The Elias Group adds menacingly, "The North State Journal - and you personally - would be liable for any such publication."

What the letter does not address is the fact that Cooper is a public figure.

In New York Times v. Sullivan, the Supreme Court crafted the actual malice standard, requiring public officials to shoulder the higher burden of proving defamation. Under that standard, an official would have to show either actual knowledge of its falsity or a reckless disregard of the truth.

The standard was later extended to public figures. The Supreme Court has held that public figure status applies when someone "thrust[s] himself into the vortex of [the] public issue [and] engage[s] the public's attention in an attempt to influence its outcome." A limited-purpose public figure status applies if someone voluntarily "draw[s] attention to himself" or allows himself to become part of a controversy "as a fulcrum to create public discussion." Wolston v. Reader's Digest Association, 443 U.S. 157, 168 (1979).

It is legally absurd to suggest that a media outlet would be liable for defamation, let alone defamation per se, for raising the mental or physical fitness of a candidate for political office.

It is indicative of Elias's sledgehammer approach that often does more harm than good for his Democratic clients. A few months ago, Elias caused a stir during the unsuccessful Democratic gerrymandering effort by reminding Democratic leaders that they could simply eliminate the entire Virginia government.

What is equally baffling is the desire of Cooper to be associated with Marc Elias while trying to appeal to Republican and independent voters. Despite his losses in cases such as National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission, Elias is still a favorite of many on the left for his aggression and partisan loyalty. What makes him notorious for some makes him popular for others.

It was Elias who was the general counsel to the Clinton presidential campaign when it secretly funded the infamous Steele dossier and pushed the false Alfa Bank conspiracy. (His fellow Perkins Coie partner, Michael Sussmann, was later indicted but acquitted).

Clinton campaign officials denied any involvement in the Steele Dossier. When journalists discovered after the election that the Clinton campaign hid payments for the Steele dossier as "legal fees" among the $5.6 million paid to Perkins Coie, they were reportedly stonewalled. The campaign was ultimately sanctioned by the Federal Election Commission for the subterfuge.

New York Times reporter Ken Vogel said at the time that Elias denied involvement in the anti-Trump dossier. When Vogel tried to report the story, he said, Elias "pushed back vigorously, saying 'You (or your sources) are wrong.'" Times reporter Maggie Haberman later wrote that "Folks involved in funding this lied about it, and with sanctimony, for a year."

Elias's group later unsuccessfully led efforts to challenge Democratic electoral losses.

In Maryland, Elias's team supported another abusive gerrymandering scheme that a court found not only violated Maryland law but the state constitution's equal protection, free speech and free elections clauses. The court found that the map "subverts the will of those governed."

One media site accused Elias and his group of "making millions off gerrymandering efforts" while publicly denouncing Republican gerrymandering.

In 2024, Elias's legal team was also accused of pushing "to bar third-party presidential candidates - including Cornel West - from swing state ballots where they might siphon votes from the Democratic nominee [Kamala Harris]."

Likewise, the New York Times reported that Elias's firm's work "on behalf of a Soros-funded PAC in Texas...was opposed by a left-leaning election watchdog as undermining laws intended to limit the influence of major donors."

His group's work for New York redistricting was ridiculed as not only ignoring the express will of the voters and also effectively negating the votes of Republican voters.

In 2024, the Chief Judge of the Western District of Wisconsin criticized the Elias Law Group for one of its challenges. Judge James Peterson (an Obama appointee) said that the argument "simply does not make any sense."

Cooper, however, wanted Elias and his legal team to represent him and must have approved threatening a media outlet rather than answering a predictable question from a journalist.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution."

title: China's iPhone Flippers Face Losses Before Apple's Foldable Even Launches
desc:
China's iPhone Flippers Face Losses Before Apple's Foldable Even Launches

Apple's first foldable iPhone, the Duo, launches in mainland China and the United States this Friday, following an October 16 preorder opening. Yet days before the first handsets even ship, Chinese speculators who lined up to flip launch-day units are already watching their expected profits evaporate.

Because the phones have not been delivered yet, this gray-market action is playing out entirely in advance resale agreements. Dealers lock in first-batch allocations during preorders and line up buyers ahead of time, with final payment and physical handoff scheduled for launch day on October 23, according to Dahe Daily.

For some middlemen, the math is already turning upside down. According to an October 19 MyDrivers report, Zhengzhou dealer Xu Shan put down a 25,000 yuan ($3,740) deposit to secure 50 iPhone Duo handsets at a total contract value of 999,950 yuan (about $149,700). Xu agreed to pay 4,000 yuan ($600) above retail per phone and planned to flip them at a 6,000 yuan ($900) markup - pocketing 2,000 yuan ($300) apiece for a target profit of 100,000 yuan ($14,970).

By October 17, however, that spread had vanished. Xu's intended buyer slashed his bid to just 3,500 yuan ($525) above retail - 500 yuan ($75) per phone below Xu's locked-in acquisition cost. Dumping all 50 handsets at that price would have handed Xu a 25,000 yuan ($3,740) loss, effectively wiping out his deposit (though not the nearly $150,000 gross order value).

Xu walked away from the bid to hunt for other buyers, leaving the loss on paper for now. Later that day, the original buyer sweetened his offer to 4,200 yuan ($630) over retail, but only for 10 phones. title: Trump Dangles $100 Million Kentucky Pharma Investment, But Only If Republicans Win Midterms
desc:
Trump Dangles $100 Million Kentucky Pharma Investment, But Only If Republicans Win Midterms

Authored by Travis Gillmore via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump announced plans for the Department of War to invest $100 million to support a pharmaceutical company, with the offer conditional on Republicans winning the midterm elections next month.

Antheia would receive the funds to boost production of ingredients used in medications at a facility in Winchester, Kentucky.

"That's a big revitalization project," Trump said during a rally in the Truist Arena at Northern Kentucky University. "But, if the Democrats win ... they wouldn't be able to do it. They wouldn't even know what you're talking about."

Details about the investment are limited. The Epoch Times reached out to the Department of War for clarification but did not receive a response prior to publication.

Trump also mentioned a billion-dollar investment between GE Appliances and the IUE-CWA union to boost manufacturing in the company's Kentucky operations, announced in September.

The president urged supporters to vote in November, calling for a high turnout in what he described as a consequential election.

"This is the most important midterm in the history of our country because we've gotten more things done, and they can undo them if we start losing an election, especially this one," Trump said. "So, pretend I'm on the ballot."

Navy SEAL veteran Republican nominee Ed Gallrein, running for the House in the state's 4th District against Democrat Melissa Strange and Libertarian Jeremy Todd, told the crowd the midterms in 17 days "could determine more than the control of Congress, it may very well determine the fate of our nation."

"This election is about far more than politics," Gallrein said. "It's about defending the principles that define our America: individual liberty, personal freedoms, faith, family, our future, and the Constitution that protects us."

He secured the nomination, with Trump's endorsement, after a hard-fought primary to unseat Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.)

Andy Barr, Republican nominee for Senate facing former state representative Democrat Charles Booker to fill the seat vacated by retiring Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), expounded on the nation's unique place in history and the sacrifices made by Americans over generations to sustain the Republic.

"On the 250th anniversary of the greatest experiment in freedom the world has ever known, we must fight to save it for the next 250 years," Barr said.

Polling data shows Gallrein and Barr with solid leads in the historically red districts.

The state's 6th Congressional District race is tighter, with Republican Ralph Alvarado, physician and former state senator, running against Democrat Zach Dembo, a former federal prosecutor.

Several thousand supporters attended the rally, with the ubiquitous Trump superfans the Front Row Joes and Blake Marnell, better known as "Mr. Wall," taking their standard positions near the front of the stage.

While most audience members were there to cheer on the president, some came with other motives.

One individual was removed after disrupting the speech, prompting Trump to say protesters "get $250" per incident.

Mother of five Nikki Reed, 62, from Virginia Beach, Virginia, drove 10 hours to the rally dressed in red, white, and blue. She said her sole purpose for attending was to infiltrate the crowd and interrupt the proceedings while Trump was speaking.

"I spent a lot of money to be here, a lot of gas money," Reed told The Epoch Times, noting an expectation for the president to dismiss her as a paid protester. "I think it's really important to say I'm not paid to be here."

She showed email receipts as evidence of dozens of donations she made to ActBlue, the donation portal for the Democratic Party.

"I pay them," Reed said, emphasizing her desire to inspire change. "There's something to be said when you're; it's almost like you're making a statement."

Security surrounded her moments after she stood on chairs and yelled "loser" while raising a jacket painted with a derogatory phrase to get the president's attention, and she was escorted away from the premises without incident.

About a dozen protesters lined the walkway near the arena, many holding signs criticizing high gas prices and inflation.

The Kentucky visit marked the president's second of the year in the state and comes on the heels of an Oct. 3 stop in Vandalia, Ohio, which shares the Cincinnati media market with his Highland Heights appearance.

Future campaign rallies announced, so far, include Wichita, Kansas; Greenville, North Carolina; Clemson, South Carolina; Sioux City, Iowa; and Fort Myers, Florida, with more stops expected through Nov. 3.

title: Cook Case Tests The Limits Of Fed Independence
desc:
Cook Case Tests The Limits Of Fed Independence

Authored by Alexander W. Salter via The Daily Economy,

President Trump has renewed his effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve Board.

Whether he has a legitimate reason to fire her is another matter. The White House announced a three-person "committee of inquiry" to investigate whether Cook made false statements on mortgage applications, and whether that is sufficient cause to remove her from her post. Next month, the committee will question her at a White House hearing.

This is Trump's second attempt. In June, the Supreme Court blocked the first one. As I wrote at the time, the ruling carved out a special exemption for the Fed. That same morning, the justices ruled in Trump v. Slaughter that agency heads who wield executive power answer to the president. Then immediately, they shielded the most powerful agency of all from the impact of that ruling.

But the June decision was narrow: Cook was entitled to notice and an opportunity to respond before removal for cause. The White House is now complying with both requirements. Cook's lawyers maintain that the alleged infraction - designating two properties as her "primary residence" - was just an "inadvertent error," pointing out that the president's and Treasury Secretary Bessent's own property filings contain the same discrepancy.

Whether the allegations around mortgage documents are proven or not, the real stakes are much bigger. President Trump's attempt to unseat Cook ultimately tests central bank independence. The conventional defense of central bank independence, reinforced by the high court's treatment established in Slaughter, holds that the Fed should be insulated from political accountability to do its job well. That doctrine deserves far more scrutiny than it usually gets.

Central bank independence rests on two claims.

The first is empirical: independent central banks supposedly deliver lower inflation. But the evidence for that is decidedly mixed, and varies with the sample and the estimation method. There's a simpler explanation that also fits the data: countries that respect the rule of law also tend to keep prices stable. Sound money comes from sound institutions, not from insulated technocrats.

The second claim is constitutional: the Fed's insulation supposedly fits within our system of separated powers. But it does not. Congress holds the power to coin money and regulate its value, and has delegated substantial power to the Fed. Many of the Fed's activities, particularly bank supervision and enforcement actions, involve the exercise of executive power. The Constitution vests the executive power in a president, who answers to voters. If central bankers who exercise that power are shielded from discipline and removal, then they answer to no one.

Milton Friedman made the fundamental argument more than 60 years ago in Capitalism and Freedom:

Mistakes, excusable or not, cannot be avoided in a system which disperses responsibility yet gives a few men great power, and which thereby makes important policy actions highly dependent on accidents of personality. This is the key technical argument against an 'independent' central bank.

An independent central bank concentrates power while diffusing responsibility. When policy fails, no one is answerable for the failure.

The Fed's recent record bears Friedman out. Following COVID-19, the central bank delivered the worst inflation in four decades. Five years later, inflation still runs above target. No one was fired, demoted, or made to face any meaningful consequence. While failing at its price stability mandate, the Fed took up projects Congress never authorized, issuing climate-risk guidance for large banks and building out DEI programming. This is what bureaucracies do when nobody can discipline them.

Cook is not a bystander here. She has served on the Board since May 2022, with inflation at 40-year highs. She attributed the Fed's inflation failures to supply constraints rather than monetary policy. And when the Board rescinded its climate guidance last fall, she formally objected. None of this constitutes "cause" in the White House's sense, and Trump's motives are doubtless partisan. But it does illustrate the deeper problem: Fed officials operate in a system where poor performance carries no penalty.

The president's committee will likely recommend firing Cook. If the president follows through, another round of litigation is likely. Remember, the problem is not a specific monetary policymaker's alleged wrongdoing. It's central bank independence itself. The solution is accountability of the ordinary kind: a limited mandate simple enough for citizens to evaluate, with meaningful consequences for poor performance. Eventually, a monetary rule could further limit officials' discretion. As Friedman put it:

The only way that has yet been suggested that offers promise is to try to achieve government of law instead of men by legislating rules for the conduct of monetary policy that will have the effect of enabling the public to exercise control over monetary policy through its political authorities, while at the same time...[preventing] monetary policy from being subject to the day-to-day whim of political authorities.

The case for central bank independence rests on a straw man. Neither Congress nor the President will set interest rates. What matters is who's ultimately in charge, especially with inflation above the Fed's target for more than five years. The American public can't afford the Fed's simultaneous concentration of power and exemption from accountability.

title: US Homebuilder Confidence Crashes To 14 Year Low, Blame Mortgage Rates & Immigration
desc:
US Homebuilder Confidence Crashes To 14 Year Low, Blame Mortgage Rates & Immigration

American homebuilder confidence crashed to 29 in October - down from 32 in September and worse than the 31 print expected as rising mortgage rates, energy and material costs, and worsening labor and lot conditions have pushed builder sentiment to a 14-year low.

All three of the major HMI indices posted losses in October.

The index measuring current sales conditions fell two points to 33, the index gauging future sales expectations dropped five points to 32 and the index charting prospective buyer traffic fell five points to 18.

“Mortgage rates have climbed well above 7% in recent weeks, and higher gas prices and inflation have further weakened buyer traffic across much of the country,” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio.

“Though builders are also contending with higher costs for construction loans, building materials and diesel, the Trump administration’s efforts to advance regulatory reform are helping to ease some of the cost pressures they face. Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work.”

Judging by Future Sales expectations, builders are not going to be adding any new supply in a hurry...

“Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges,” said NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz.

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines. As a result, buyer traffic has fallen to its lowest level since April 2012, excluding the pandemic’s onset in April 2020.”

The latest HMI survey found that 43% of builders cut prices in October, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period.

The average price cut remained at 6% for the seventh consecutive month. Meanwhile, 65% of builders reported using sales incentives in October, the 19th straight month at least 60% of builders have done so.

Looking at the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped one point to 38, the Midwest fell three points to 40, the South fell one point to 30 and the West posted a two-point decline to 26.

However, as ugly as the data was, builder confidence has a long way to go before it catches down to homebuyer confidence...

Homebuyers have never been less enthusiastic about the American Dream... perhaps this is why...

The gap between current mortgage rates (7.5%) and the average mortgage across all of American homeowners (4.33%) is extreme to say the least, trapping sellers and buyers...

title: Democracy Manifest
desc:
Democracy Manifest

By Benjamin Picton, senior market strategist at Rabobank

US stocks defied a strong lead from Europe and Asia on Friday to close broadly in the red. IT, telecommunications and the consumer discretionary sector led declines while energy, materials and consumer staples performed well. Oil prices surged following further reports of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran claiming that two tankers carrying up to 4 million barrels of crude were struck by marine mines. The BBC reports UKMTO figures noting that the number of ships being attacked in and around the Strait hit a new high of 12 vessels in the week to the 11th of October.

Rising oil prices helped to see ten-year Treasury yields close 1.5bps higher at 5.07% after a big drop on Thursday. Two-year yields fell by 3bps, causing a steepening of the yield curve that might have provided a slight tailwind to financial stocks. Higher oil prices and rising long yields were not helpful for the consumer discretionary sector that was perhaps still trading off the signal of a weaker-than-expected retail sales report released the day before, which gave the impression that spending on automotive fuels is cannibalising demand for other goods.

Following market close on Friday news emerged that President Trump is enacting a waiver of steep Graham Act sanctions and tariffs that were due to come into effect. The Act requires the imposition of secondary sanctions in the form of 100% tariffs against the top five buyers of Russian crude oil and gas products while also placing 500% tariffs on Russian energy products being imported into the United States. Active Brent crude futures are down by $1.80/bbl at time of writing.

Depending on how the calculation is performed, the top five buyers of Russian energy products are likely to include China, India, Turkey and the European Union. The imposition of 100% tariffs on China would certainly torpedo the truce in the trade war that was extended to January only a few weeks ago and would risk a response in the form of renewed export restrictions on rare earth minerals. 100% tariffs on the EU and Turkey would be a major strike against NATO allies at a time when the Trump administration wants Europe to contribute more to collective defence and Turkey to play ball with US interests in the Middle East. Striking India would antagonize an emerging great power that the USA would like to use as a geopolitical counterweight to China in the Indo-Pacific, an investor in new US production, and a customer for US defence and nuclear energy exports.

Of course, the imposition of Graham Act sanctions would also directly contradict recent efforts of the administration to reduce fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. Relations between Moscow and Washington appear to be in an upturn following the recent controversial deal for the US to import Russian diesel sanctions-free over the coming months. That deal drew condemnation from Ukraine and several members of congress, as did Friday’s decision to waive the Graham Act sanctions. In a post to Truth Social on Sunday President Trump said that his decision was aimed at avoiding anything that will “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated over the weekend that the waiver was only for a period of 60 days to give the US time to “analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even the US economy”. Some might detect an implied threat that while buyers of Russian energy have avoided the sanctions for the time being, the Sword of Damocles still hangs, and the administration now has greater powers to coerce other countries into doing what it wants.

Rubio’s 60 days would expire after the midterm elections, which is the line in the sand that President Trump has repeatedly nominated when saying that the US would not engage in fresh strikes against Iran before that date. Once the midterms are out of the way, it looks like all bets are off and we can expect a dramatic ramping up in geopolitical volatility. That impression was seemingly confirmed last Thursday when President Trump again implied in an interview with Newsmax that the United States was considering striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain complex, where nuclear centrifuges from the Natanz site are thought to have been relocated.

An IRGC spokesman said in a post on X that any attack on Iranian energy infrastructure would trigger a “scorched earth” response against Israel, with other Iranian sources suggesting a ‘nuclear for nuclear’ attack on Israeli reactors if Pickaxe Mountain were to be struck. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu – freshly endorsed for re-election at next week’s poll by Donald Trump – said that the Islamic Republic must be toppled and that he had directed Israel’s security agencies to pursue that goal, without US support if necessary.

While the world grapples with the energy shock emanating from hot wars in Europe and the Middle East, French President Macron continues to grapple with political unrest at home. Tensions ran high over the weekend as widespread protests erupted into rioting and looting, with images of the burning of the historic town hall in Limoges circulating on social media and about 1000 police officers reported injured.

President Macron said in an address to the nation that a distinction must be drawn between the actions of the rioters and the legitimate concerns of protestors demonstrating against rising living costs and decaying public services. Marine Le Pen, the right-wing frontrunner for the upcoming presidential election, railed against what she called “exhausted Macronist power” saying that France faces a crisis of confidence and authority that now poses a threat to democracy.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar echoed sentiments expressed by Donald Trump blaming the riots on uncontrolled immigration, claiming that the scenes in France vindicated Hungary’s tough approach. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk – avoiding explicit mention of France -similarly extolled the virtues of his own country’s hardline stance on immigration, saying that Poland would “neither repeat nor pay for” other countries’ mistakes. The Euro is this morning trading lower despite a broad US Dollar selloff.

Keeping with the theme of democracy, today is an important date in the Canadian province of Alberta. A non-binding referendum will be held where voters are asked to indicate whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or commence the constitutional process to secede. Voters will also be asked a series of questions about their views on control of immigration, voter ID, and to what degree non-citizens should have recourse to public healthcare and other social programs.

Needless to say, the results of the vote will be closely watched in Ottawa, and in Washington D.C.

By Eric Peters, CIO of One River Asset Management

Colosseums

“Classic late cycle,” said Sparks. “Beginning of the end, that’s what’s unfolding,” said the investor, entrepreneur, iconoclast. “At the end, everything converges to financial flows.” In every huge cycle, the last stage is Ponzi-like. “Who’s going to buy the last CDO? Who’s going to buy the last CDO-squared? How do those securities even work? That’s what happens in these cycles. The last securities to be issued are the most complex and hardest to understand. They’re the riskiest,” he said. “The cost of capital starts going up. This is how it always ends.”

“You saw the Aussie data center IPO [here] that failed this week, right?” asked Sparks. “It’s their neocloud equivalent, like CoreWeave, it’s the type of sign we saw when the Bear Stearns hedge funds failed.” Summer of 2007. “Some of the marginal deals will not pencil anymore.” And that slows the whole machine down. “When that happens, investors go from the fear of missing out to the fear of holding the bag. That’s a process, it doesn’t happen overnight, but by the time these sorts of things are glaringly obvious, it’s too late, checkmate.”

“When the process starts in earnest, it becomes self-fulfilling, irreversible,” explained Sparks. “That’s really the point in investing, finding processes that once set in motion lead to a predictable outcome.” Even if the timing remains uncertain. “Someone buys a bond that funds a Meta data center. Now it’s trading at 88 cents. And then you read Anthropic just offered Blackstone a yield of over 10% to fund its datacenter.” Four months ago, Anthropic funded at 8.5%. “So, you take your loss and the bond volatility into account, and you’re not eager to buy.”

“These dynamics slow the flywheel,” continued Sparks. “The greater fool theory starts to reverse and self-perpetuates.” I nodded. “Everyone wants to know exactly when it will fall,” he said. “On some level it doesn’t really matter, because once the process starts, you pretty much know stocks won’t massively blow through the highs.” The rough ceiling on the market is in place. “You don’t have to worry about the FOMO move that rips 30% higher and makes you look foolish. So, instead, you can build a portfolio for the sacking and looting ahead.”

“Once the cost of capital rises for the weaker players, you crack the hidden pillars supporting the edifice,” said Sparks. “It’s like removing the little fasteners holding the structure together.” The Roman Colosseum flashed through my mind, its structure originally secured by 300 metric tons of iron clamps. But after Rome fell, thieves stole the metal, which in turn weakened the arena, and it succumbed to earthquakes. “That’s why a major top is a process, it takes time to undermine the structure. And it all ends when the Generals are killed.”

Anecdote

“What do you want to accomplish in capitalism?” asked Sparks, not waiting for a response. “You want to spend as little money as possible to create the biggest monopoly you can. That’s literally all you want to do. Nothing more.”

Fair point. “You can talk about adoption and demand curves all you want, and it’s not that they’re unimportant, but they tell you less about whether you have a good business and more about the size of your net worth as a monopolist.”

Owning a big monopoly is better than a small one but having a baby monopoly is better than running a big business in a fiercely competitive industry with razor thin margins. “Everyone loves Amazon, but if you strip out its AWS and advertising businesses, it’s really just a retailer and logistics company, and those are generally low margin, capital intensive businesses,” he said.

“And yes, there are some elements of Amazon retail that are monopolistic but compare it to Google - that’s a real monopoly, with massive margins.” Amazon’s retail business is probably worth roughly the same as Walmart at $1trln. Google is worth $4trln. “So what will these AI companies look like on the other side of this rapid build out?” Amazon retail or Google?

“Even if you make the argument that everything in our economy will eventually be turned into AI tokens in one form or another, so that token demand will be explosive, why do you think that the frontier labs will be the real beneficiaries?” asked Sparks. “From the days when we first commercialized electricity to today, global usage has exploded. But owning utilities has not been the way to make your fortune.” Indeed.

“The nature of this technology and the transformation of electricity into tokens looks a lot more like the utilities than something that will manifest into durable monopolies. And I think that as this cycle matures, if we survive as a species, we’ll find that the real beneficiaries will be the users of tokens, not the AI companies that manufacture them.”

title: Futures Rise As Dip Buyers Rush Back Into Chips After Worst Nasdaq Week Since Liberation Day
desc:
Futures Rise As Dip Buyers Rush Back Into Chips After Worst Nasdaq Week Since Liberation Day

US futures are higher - but well off session highs hit before the European open - as dip buyers storm back into chipmakers after the Nasdaq's worst week since the April 2025 tariff turmoil, while oil slides after President Trump waived Russian sanctions to seal a diesel deal and Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Persian Gulf flows have recovered to about 80% of pre-conflict levels; as a result Nasdaq futures are up more than 1% and the Philly semis index is set to snap its longest losing streak in 18 years, even as Europe slides on a weekend of riots in France. As of 8:00am ET, S&P futures were 0.4% higher at 7,741.75 while Nasdaq futures rose 1.1% to 29,705.50 and Dow futures are down 0.2%. That follows a Friday session in which the S&P fell 1.09% to 7,659 (sliding from flat just before the European close), the Nasdaq 100 sank 2.5% and the SOX tumbled 3.8% for an eighth straight loss, capping a week in which the SOX lost 11.4%, the Nasdaq 4.5% and CoreWeave a quarter of its value. In premarket trading, semis lead with Intel up 4.2% on a JPMorgan upgrade and Nvidia up 1.4%, neoclouds and optical names are bid (CoreWeave +6% after a Goldman upgrade from Neutral ($139PT) to Buy ($106PT?!) week in which it became "the market's beta barometer"), Disc Medicine soars 35% ahead of Phase 3 data and Cleveland-Cliffs jumps 13% after an earnings beat. The day's driver is Washington's Russia pivot: Trump signed an executive order waiving Graham Act sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russian energy revenues (Russia will initially supply over 300k tonnes of diesel), Putin proposed a summit with Trump and Xi to negotiate an end to the war, and Zelenskyy accused Trump of pressuring Kyiv to surrender, which has sent Brent down 1.2% to $108.59. Treasuries dip slightly with shorter-dated yields edging higher in a bear flattener as traders keep a muted bid for an October hike, leaving the 10Y at 5.08% after last week's 16.5bp plunge (its biggest weekly drop since August 2025), while French bonds tumble after the riots, with the OAT-Bund spread widening to 146bps. The dollar index is up 0.1% to 101.93, with the euro the G10 laggard below $1.12 and the Aussie leading after strong Chinese data. In commodities, WTI is little changed near $101.30, European gas (Dutch TTF) hit its highest since 2022, gold is up 0.1% at $4,169 and silver adds 0.9% to $57.49. Bitcoin rises 2.5% to about $82,850 after briefly topping $83,000. US economic data slate includes the October NAHB housing market index (10am). The Fed is in its external communications blackout through Oct. 29, so there are no Fed speakers. The Treasury sells $95 billion of 13-week and $82 billion of 26-week bills at 11:30am.

In premarket trading, Nvidia outperforms Magnificent Seven peers as chip stocks look set to rebound: Nvidia (NVDA) +1.4%, Amazon (AMZN) +1.2%, Alphabet (GOOGL) +0.6%, Meta Platforms (META) +0.2%, Microsoft (MSFT) +0.2%, Tesla (TSLA) -0.1%, Apple (AAPL) -0.1%

  • Semiconductor stocks gain, setting the chip benchmark up to snap its longest losing streak in 18 years. Shares in neoclouds and optical firms are also rising amid a broad-based rally in AI-related firms.
  • Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF) rises 13% after the steel producer reported adjusted Ebitda for the third quarter that beat the average analyst estimate.
  • Disc Medicine (IRON) soars 63% after announcing that its investigational drug bitopertin met all primary and secondary endpoints in the Phase 3 Apollo trial in adults and adolescents with erythropoietic protoporphyria.
  • Intel (INTC) rises 3% as JPMorgan upgrades its rating to neutral (with a PT of $85 or below where it closed on Friday), noting that the chipmaker’s turnaround might take years, but the management’s execution has been solid.
  • Silgan (SLGN) gains 5% after the food packaging company and funds affiliated with American Industrial Partners announced a deal to buy Trivium Packaging in an all-cash deal.
  • Pinterest (PINS) gains 1.1% as Phillip Securities initiates coverage with a recommendation of buy, noting that the company has significant international monetization potential.
  • Disc Medicine (IRON) jumps 35% ahead of the company’s webcast to discuss topline results from the APOLLO Phase 3 trial of Bitopertin in erythropoietic protoporphyria.
  • BYD US (+1.4%): Boyd Gaming shares rise as Morgan Stanley upgrades to overweight from equal-weight following a selloff across gaming stocks.
  • RCAT US (+6.4%): Red Cat rises after the US drone and robot maker offered a 29% cash premium to buy Austrian engine specialist Steyr Motors, in order to boost its European defense portfolio.

In other corporate news, Anthropic, apparently undeterred by a week in which the market discovered that AI costs money to fund, is offering Blackstone a yield above 10% to anchor a $60 billion TPU-backed debt package (per JPMorgan's desk), and separately said it will put 5% of its shares into a new public benefit fund. Nvidia-backed Nscale faces investor pushback over its IPO valuation after Microsoft exited its UK data center deal, as we reported over the weekend. Silgan is said to be near a $3.4 billion purchase of Trivium Packaging; KKR is selling Infinity Transportation to Ares for about $2.9 billion (WSJ); SoftBank is said to weigh buying top US security firm Allied; Starboard sees value in Apple chip supplier Skyworks; and Accenture is working on a potential sale of its China business that could value the unit at up to $1.5 billion (FT). Oaktree's deal to take over a life insurer owned by Advantage Capital has collapsed after regulators raised alarms over exposure to 777 Partners. EQT agreed to buy Australia's Cleanaway Waste Management for about A$9.3 billion including debt. Red Cat offered to buy Steyr Motors for EUR 39 a share in cash, and Ivanhoe Electric is in advanced talks to sell its US copper assets. Kimberly-Clark could kick off this week's IG issuance as its Kenvue acquisition nears closing, while Citigroup and Wells Fargo launched their first euro bond deals of the year. Elon Musk pledged to give one SpaceX share to "every kid in America" next year, and Hyperscale Data plans to take its AI subsidiary askROI public.

Stock futures are rebounding from the Nasdaq's worst week since the tariff turmoil of April 2025, with dip buyers stepping in after the tech index broke below its closely watched 10- and 20-week moving averages; this week's earnings from Netflix, Tesla and Meta (which UBS hinted may have pulled its earnings a week sooner as it may be raising capital ahead of its peers) will provide the next test for the still-shaky AI trade. The bounce comes as bond yields stabilize and oil pulls back below $100 (at least for a bit), and on the 39th anniversary of Black Monday, which DB's Jim Reid notes is a "more memorable one" since it falls on a Monday. Yet as is so often the case, markets keep doing what they're not supposed to: Friday brought what Goldman's desk called record put buying and the "first real sign of panic in index protection" (as we detailed), even as retail poured a record amount into levered ETFs, and the S&P barely flinched while Morgan Stanley's AI basket suffered its worst week ever.

The Nasdaq 100 now needs to reclaim 30,000: the slide below 30K unwound the October breakout and cost the Nasdaq its 10 and 20-week moving averages; futures point to a sharp rebound, making 30K the first hurdle for bulls, with the 40-week moving average near 27.5K the next major support if it fails.

JPMorgan's Mislav Matejka says that a stabilization in bond yields would "go a long way to support stocks" if it continues, especially given concerns over AI financing costs. Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson advised that investors should prepare to add risk, reiterating a preference for quality stocks, while Citi strategists say tech is still set to account for nearly 70% of global earnings growth next year, making this week's results a key gauge of whether Monday's bounce can become something more durable.

“Asia’s cash markets are catching up with Friday’s Wall Street selloff,” said Anna Wu, founder of Floodlines Research in Sydney. “Investors want more evidence that AI spending is translating into returns. Until then, Asia’s chip-heavy markets remain particularly exposed to swings in that conviction.”

Hedging demand, meanwhile, has gone vertical: S&P 500 puts are getting bid up, with the normalized 3-month put skew reaching the highest since late July, after trading near the lows of the past two years as recently as the beginning of this month.

JPM's Market Intel desk under Andrew Tyler admits last week's selloff "ran against our tactical bullish call," but after reassessing, the team retains its tactically bullish stance, albeit "more selective": the momentum/tech unwind and AI credit fears drove the selloff while ASML and TSMC delivered healthy earnings and consumer data stayed resilient. JPM does not expect the rotation out of tech to end abruptly, and favors cyclicals outside tech while selectively buying semis and memory weakness via defined-risk options; all eyes are on Meta earnings and Nvidia's GTC Berlin. JPM credit strategist Nathaniel Rosenbaum notes hyperscaler spreads widened 12bp last week to 148bp, the widest since July, but sees the widening as overdone unless earnings reveal fundamental weakness. JPM credit trader Christian Crosby was less sanguine: the funding cost concerns "are now more about levered borrowers, specifically neoclouds, data center project finance, and GPU deals," where "every point higher in borrowing costs is worth multiple points on the equity."

Over at Goldman, Tony Pasquariello writes that "we've entered a new phase in the AI sequence, one that is unequivocally more complicated (for both the credit market and the equity market)," and that "for the first time in three years, a number of key asset markets have felt the 'speed limit' from the bond market" (on which more here). Goldman's Prime book saw the largest net selling of tech on record, with US long/short net leverage down to 43.7%, a 5-year low, and shorts near 5-year highs, which is why Lee Coppersmith thinks "the market is moving into a different volatility environment but not necessarily a more bearish one." GS flow trader Giulio Esposito flags a "sharp rotation out of AI hardware into real-economy defensives," with the equal-weight S&P beating the cap-weighted index by 225bp last week, the most since November 2020, while Sam Dunn reckons "the AI trade is still long but roughly 6/10 on length and materially cleaner than Jun/July."

In geopolitics, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy accused Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Russia, escalating a week-long row. Trump wrote on social media over the weekend that he cut a diesel export deal with Russia and delayed imposing further sanctions because he doesn't want to drive Putin away from peace talks, and Republican lawmakers, including some of the president's strongest allies, blasted Trump over the sanctions waiver (Moscow, for its part, celebrated a "historic moment"). In global news, China's growth accelerated more than expected in the third quarter, boosting the odds of the economy reaching Beijing's annual target and dimming the prospects for additional easing measures.

In France, cost-of-living protests degenerated into looting and burning nationwide over the weekend, with nearly 2,400 arrests and almost 1,000 police injured, and protests also took place in Italy, Belgium and Portugal. Ten-year OAT yields are up more than 9bps to about 4.90%, with the OAT-Bund spread widening to 146bps, not far from the recent 151bps peak and just days before Moody's review on Friday. Macron appealed for calm but stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, which Reid warns "won't make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 0.7% at around 640, with 478 members down and just 103 up, as France's CAC 40 leads declines after the weekend's violence; the CAC 40 and Spain's IBEX 35 are both down 1.3% and Italy's FTSE MIB 1.4%. Banks are the sector laggard, followed by travel & leisure and autos, while tech and energy are the only sectors in the green. JPM's desk notes weakness is broad, with autos, industrials, basic resources, banks and utilities lagging. Defense names are lower, with BAE, Thales and Leonardo all down more than 2.5%, while Norwegian energy names hit 52-week highs. Here are the biggest European movers:

  • Verbio shares rise as much as 4.2% following remarks from the German transport minister, cited by Augsburger Allgemeine, who floated the idea of using fuel containing up to a fifth of ethanol.
  • Mowi shares rise as much as 5.2% to a six-month high after the salmon-farming company reported earnings well ahead of expectations thanks to record harvest volumes in the latest quarter.
  • Pets at Home shares gain as much as 5.7% after Peel Hunt upgrades the retailer to buy from hold on signs that trading and execution are improving.
  • French stocks underperform after cost-of-living protests over the weekend.
  • DHL shares fall as much as 2.3% after the German logistics company reported preliminary third-quarter earnings, which Morgan Stanley said may augur more muted growth in the future.
  • Imperial Brands falls as much as 2.1% after being downgraded at Jefferies. The bank thinks the tobacco company could fail to impress investors with its FY27 guidance due to slower growth in Germany.

Asian stocks were mixed, extending tech-led losses from the previous week before paring them as US futures rebounded: the MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell as much as 1%, with chipmakers SK Hynix, TSMC and Advantest among the top decliners as DeepSeek's latest model sparked concerns over demand for chips. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.6% after last week's 5.4% slide, while South Korea's Kospi staged an impressive comeback, rising 1.8% after plunging as much as 3.2% at the open. Taiwan's Taiex slid 1.8% in early trading and the Taiwan dollar fell to its weakest since April 2025 on stock outflows. The CSI 300 rose 0.1% after China's Q3 GDP grew 4.5% y/y (vs 4.4% expected) and September retail sales doubled expectations, while Australia's ASX 200 gained 0.4%, led by Cleanaway, which jumped as much as 21% after EQT agreed to buy it. Hong Kong was closed for the Chung Yeung Festival. Indonesia's rout deepened, with stocks down more than 5% to a six-year low and more than 16% in two sessions after MSCI warned of a potential two-step downgrade; Goldman estimates a full removal from MSCI indexes could trigger about $5.6 billion of passive outflows.

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is little changed while the DXY is up 0.1% to 101.93, at the upper end of a 101.76-102.08 range. The euro is the G10 laggard, slipping below 1.12 (to the middle of a 1.1182-1.1234 range) on the French unrest, and speculative euro positioning is already the most pessimistic in a decade. The Aussie outperforms, rising 0.5% to 0.6977 after China's data beat, and the loonie is also firmer after Trump touted an "amazing" deal with Canada at some point. USD/JPY is back around 158.10, while EUR/CHF dropped 0.4% to a fresh three-month low of 0.92264.

In rates, Treasuries dip slightly, with shorter-dated yields edging higher and the curve bear flattening as traders maintain a muted expectation for an October hike: the 10Y is up about 1bp to 5.08% and the 2Y is at 4.73%, while money markets assign a 14% chance of a hike next week and 75% for December. That follows last week's 16.5bp drop in the 10Y, its biggest weekly decline since August 2025, as the AI growth scare revived the haven bid even as hot CPI and PPI prints should have done the opposite (we are told this is normal). In Europe, OATs are hit by over 70 ticks as the French riots push the OAT-Bund spread to 146bps, BTPs are down around 25 ticks on protests in Italy, and gilts are down almost 50 ticks on spillover selling, while Bunds are flat around 3.44%. The Treasury sells $95 billion of 13-week and $82 billion of 26-week bills today, and dealers expect about $25 billion of IG issuance this week, which would leave 2026 less than $10 billion short of the record set in 2020.

“Yields above 5% provide far more income protection against being early, while a meaningful growth shock would bring capital gains on top,” writes Bloomberg macro strategist Skylar Montgomery Koning. “Last week’s willingness to buy the dip in bonds suggests the market is starting to recognise that trade-off.”

In commodities, oil retreats from a five-month high, with Brent down 1.2% to $108.59 and WTI little changed at $101.30, as traders book profits after a blistering rally and Trump's Russia sanctions waiver frees up diesel supply; the US is also negotiating with European allies to release diesel stockpiles and the DoE issued an RFP to exchange up to 17 million barrels of SPR crude. The Middle East remains tense, however: the IRGC said two tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting mines, and explosions were reported in Jeddah after Houthi attacks. Dutch TTF gas rose to its highest since 2022, trading in a EUR 87.66-89.32/MWh range. Spot gold is contained in a $4,155-4,190 band, silver is up about 1%, and LME copper hit $14,480/t on the China data before falling back to $14,350/t. US natgas is up 0.6% to $3.14.

US economic data slate includes the October NAHB housing market index (10am). There are no Fed speakers as the FOMC is in blackout ahead of the Oct. 27-28 meeting. Cleveland-Cliffs and Fifth Third report before the open, with Zions, Crown Holdings, W R Berkley, FNB, RLI, Western Alliance, Steel Dynamics, BOK Financial, AGNC and Wintrust after the close; the week ahead brings Netflix on Tuesday, Meta and Tesla on Wednesday, and Nvidia's GTC Berlin from Oct. 20-22.

Market Snapshot

Top Overnight News

  • Intensifying concerns about the cost and availability of funding have caused investors to reduce their equity market exposures and price a deceleration in the growth outlook. Rising energy prices and interest rates have weighed on the performance of many cyclical equities since early August. During the last two weeks, however, the potential implications of a sharply rising cost of capital on the AI build-out have weighed further on the market outlook for economic and earnings growth. Exacerbating these rotations, this week GS Prime Services noted a sharp reduction in hedge fund net leverage alongside a positioning pullback in AI-related stocks. GIR
  • Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang took a sanguine view toward the latest AI stock-market rout, saying the benefits of the technology will soon outweigh the concerns of investors. BBG
  • President Trump, defending his decision to ease tariffs and other sanctions against Russia, said on Sunday that he was making “great progress” in a peace deal with the Kremlin and suggested for the first time that the process included “hostage negotiations.” NYT
  • Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed that he, President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet next month to talk about Ukraine in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year conflict that would favor Moscow, said people familiar with the discussions. WSJ
  • Washington is pushing an idea whereby Europe would resume buying Russian gas an inducement for Putin to end the war in Ukraine. NYT
  • Iranian support has helped the Houthis mount the most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies, including help targeting drone and missile attacks, as well as training, intelligence and tactical guidance, people briefed on intelligence from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s anti-Houthi alliance said. WSJ
  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Donald Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Russia, escalating a week-long row with the US president. BBG
  • Republican lawmakers, including some of the president’s strongest allies on Capitol Hill, blasted Donald Trump for waiving new tariffs and sanctions on Russia, prompting the president to defend himself against members of his own party. BBG
  • US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News that Persian Gulf oil flows had recovered to about 80% of their pre-conflict level, although refined-product shipments remained constrained. Wright said he’s in talks with European allies to release diesel stockpiles. BBG
  • China’s growth accelerated more than expected last quarter, putting Beijing’s annual target within reach and dimming the prospects for further easing measures. GDP expanded 4.5% year on year. BBG
  • Apple on Friday said its foldable iPhone Duo had seen “nothing short of extraordinary” demand, as the device sold out on the company’s website until next year within hours of going on sale. FT
  • The US government’s debt interest burden reached a record high for fiscal 2026, with net interest costs coming to $1.05 trillion, up more than 8% from the $970 billion in fiscal 2025. BBG
  • Elon Musk pledged to give one SpaceX share to “every kid in America” next year. BBG
  • Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterm elections. NBC
  • Nvidia-backed data center developer Nscale faces opposition to the valuation target it’s pursuing in its IPO, according to people familiar with the matter. BBG
  • The violence that rocked France this weekend as cost-of-living protests degenerated into looting and burning nationwide is raising alert levels across Europe, where elections will be held in at least half a dozen countries next year. BBG
  • Indonesian markets extended their selloff, with stocks deepening their worst rout in almost 30 years and losses spreading to bonds and the rupiah after MSCI Inc. warned the country may face a two-step downgrade. BBG
  • China’s financial regulators are establishing a liquidity support facility to cushion non-bank financial institutions against potential large scale redemption pressures, People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng said at the Financial Street Forum annual meeting in Beijing, CCTV reported. BBG
  • The Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders misrepresented illiquid private credit loans to understate their risk after the Prudential Regulation Authority received a complaint earlier this year. FT
  • IRGC said two oil tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting mines. Newsquawk
  • US President Trump pledged USD 5k for every adult if the GOP wins Congress, speaking at a Kentucky rally ahead of the 3rd November midterms; separately, Reuters reported he blamed aides for a faltering Republican midterm strategy as Democrats led House polls. Newsquawk
  • JPM credit strategist Nathaniel Rosenbaum notes hyperscaler spreads widened 12bp last week to 148bp, the widest since July 2026, but sees the widening as overdone unless upcoming earnings reveal fundamental weakness. JPM

A more detailed look at global markets courtesy of Newsquawk

APAC stocks were mixed following Friday's tech-led sell-off on Wall Street, with Japanese and Korean stocks underperforming amid continued pressure on AI and semiconductor names. However, losses were pared as US equity futures recovered alongside a pullback in crude prices. Sentiment was also supported by Trump's latest Russia-Ukraine peace efforts and easing of restrictions on Russian energy, while Chinese activity data generally topped expectations but prompted little reaction. ASX 200 bucked the regional weakness, supported by Cleanaway Waste Management surging after EQT agreed to acquire the Co. Elsewhere, RBA's Kent noted evidence of rising neutral interest rates in Australia and abroad. Nikkei 225 and KOSPI underperformed as tech stocks caught up with Friday's losses in their US counterparts, although the indices pared earlier losses of over 2%. For Japan, BoJ Governor Ueda also spoke overnight but offered little fresh. Shanghai Comp was marginally softer despite Chinese activity data generally topping expectations, although Fixed Asset Investment remained weak. Hang Seng was closed for the Chung Yeung Festival.

Top Asian News

  • China PBoC Governor said overnight open-market repo rate will become the main policy rate, with a potential shift to overnight open-market operations to improve interest-rate regulation. The Governor added that monetary policy framework reform will remain gradual and ongoing, and plans to widen access to standing lending facility, introduce a liquidity tool for non-bank institutions and pilot further facilitation of onshore RMB purchases and sales by overseas financial institutions.
  • China's Stats Bureau said the economy showed more positive developments in Jan-Sept, though weak demand and a complex international environment remain challenges; its Deputy Head said new growth drivers, including high-end manufacturing and the digital economy, accounted for over 40% of growth, while consumption contributed 46.7% of GDP growth.
  • Japanese PM Takaichi said the government has no predetermined plans on whether to compile a supplementary budget and a robust economy can boost market confidence in the JPY; her approval rating fell below 50%, the lowest since she took office, Kyodo reported.

European bourses (STOXX 600 -0.8%) are broadly lower to start the week, as Dutch TTF rises to its highest level since 2022. Top European News

FX

  • EUR/USD is currently underperforming vs peers; it fell beneath the 1.12 mark, to currently trade at the midpoint of a 1.1182-1.1234 range.   • The Aussie is the clear outperformer this morning, taking positive leads from strong Chinese Activity Data overnight.   • More interestingly, the Governor mentioned that the open market overnight reverse repo rate will correspondingly become the main policy rate. He said it would be inappropriate to signal in advance when the BoJ might conduct emergency bond market operations, with any intervention to depend on the speed of long-term rate rises and signs of market instability; long-term rates would likely rise steadily in line with policy rate hikes, financial conditions remain accommodative and fiscal spending is adding upward pressure on prices and wages.
  • RBA Assistant Governor Kent said there is reasonable evidence neutral rates are rising in Australia and abroad, and that policy is somewhat restrictive but it is questionable whether it is restrictive enough; household demand is softening while business credit remains strong, and housing tax adjustments move policy in a favourable direction. Fixed Income

39 years ago today we woke up to the origins of what would forever be known as Black Monday, where the Dow fell -22.6% on the day. It’s rare the anniversary falls on a Monday so it’s a more memorable one today. The late US trading session on Friday almost felt people were worried we'd get a repeat today as the S&P fell from flat just before the European close to -1.09% by the US one. However, this morning we are seeing a bounce with S&P (+0.79%) and Nasdaq (+1.29%) futures making up most of their late Friday losses.

Clearly the main nervousness last week was around AI-related names, with credit markets starting to show some distress in that sector. The Philly semiconductor index was down -11.41% last week (-3.83% Friday), whilst the NASDAQ was down -4.48% (-2.14% Friday). At the heart of the sell-off was CoreWeave, which was down -25.21% last week (-11.91% Friday), whilst their 5yr CDS was up +225bps on the week to 1128bps with their cash bonds trading at around a 15% yield. Meanwhile, Oracle’s share price was down -9.31% (-4.64% Friday), and their 5yr CDS was up +44bps on the week to 300bps.

Asia has started the week relatively calm with the KOSPI (+0.55%) and S&P/ASX 200 (+0.32%) both trading higher, while the CSI 300 (+0.09%) and Shanghai Composite (+0.16%) are just above flat. The Nikkei (-0.73%) is the region’s weakest performer, extending losses after falling -5.4% last week as technology stocks came under heavy pressure. Elsewhere, Indonesia’s benchmark stock index is down more than 5% to its lowest level in six years, as concerns over the potential MSCI downgrade we discussed on Friday continues to heighten fears of further foreign investor outflows. The index is down over -16% in these past two sessions.

Early morning data showed that China’s economic expansion accelerated marginally in the third quarter of 2026, with real GDP growing by +4.5% y/y. This print slightly surpassed the consensus expectation of +4.4% and marked a modest step up from the +4.3% expansion recorded in the second quarter. On a sequential basis, GDP grew by +1.2% q/q outperforming the +1.1% forecast and accelerating from +0.9% in the prior period. The quarterly performance was primarily underpinned by resilient export volumes and robust demand within the artificial intelligence infrastructure supply chain.

Separately, China's September activity indicators were on the decent side. Industrial production rose by +5.5% y/y, beating expectations of +5.4% and accelerating from +5.2% in August. On the demand side, consumer spending showed signs of firming as retail sales expanded by +1.1% y/y - more than double the consensus forecast of +0.5% and a notable improvement from the +0.4% growth recorded in August.

Elsewhere, France’s political and fiscal problems gained another complication over the weekend as nationwide cost-of-living protests descended into some of the country’s worst unrest in years. Around 550,000 people demonstrated on Saturday according to the Interior Ministry, although the CGT put the figure at 800,000, and the violence continued into Sunday with fresh clashes in Paris and Marseille. The latest official figures put arrests at 2,400 and police injuries at nearly 1,000. This won't make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs, so the modest recovery in French spreads over the last week or so will be tested today. In a televised address last night, President Macron appealed for calm, saying France felt “anger and shame” at the violence. He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, but said prefects could ban protests where necessary to protect public buildings and businesses, while distinguishing peaceful demonstrators from ultra-left groups and criminals blamed by the government for the rioting. With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets. OAT futures are down around a third of a percent in price terms this morning as other DM bond futures are flat to slightly higher so there has been some small impact so far.

The week ahead doesn’t really have a big focal point but instead a broad global range of releases, with the flash October PMIs on Friday providing the first coordinated read on activity across the US, UK, Japan and the major euro-area economies. Before then, the UK has a busy run of labour-market data tomorrow and inflation on Wednesday. Japan’s national CPI arrives on Friday, while Canada also has inflation data today. Central-bank action is quieter, with the Bank of Korea deciding on Thursday and the Fed already in its communications blackout ahead of next week’s FOMC. Earnings season also broadens out, with Netflix tomorrow and Meta and Tesla on Wednesday among the highlights. We have 76 S&P 500 and 69 Stoxx 600 companies releasing with next week being even larger.

In the US, the calendar itself is relatively light, which should leave markets continuing to digest last week’s much stronger-than-expected inflation numbers. Headline CPI rose +0.65% in September, taking the annual rate from 3.4% to 3.7%, while core CPI increased +0.33%, with its annual rate up two-tenths to 2.6%. The important point was that the upside surprise was broad-based across core goods, shelter and services rather than being driven by one idiosyncratic component. PPI was also stronger than expected on Thursday, and our economists’ current tracking for September core PCE is +0.36% month-on-month, or about 3.14% year-on-year absent revisions. So there is plenty for the Fed to consider even though officials are now in blackout.

As for this week’s US releases, the housing data come first. Our economists expect the NAHB housing-market index to slip to 31 from 32 today. Tomorrow, our economists expect housing starts to rise to an annualised 1.300mn from 1.275mn, while building permits are expected at 1.400mn versus 1.403mn previously. Large surprises could still shift estimates of Q3 activity, with our economists continuing to expect annualised real GDP growth of 3.3%. More broadly, they expect inflation-adjusted output to expand 2.5% on a Q4/Q4 basis in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027.

Later in the week, our economists expect initial jobless claims to rise to 206k from 199k on Thursday. The main US releases then come with the flash S&P Global PMIs on Friday, where our economists expect manufacturing to ease to 55.5 from 55.9 and services to 57.5 from 58.8. These numbers have recently mattered for markets: the sharp rise in the September PMIs helped drive an almost 15bp increase in both 2yr and 10yr Treasury yields on September 23. Our economists still expect the Fed to remain on hold at next week’s October meeting, allowing policymakers more time to assess the underlying inflation trend and the tightening in financial conditions from the recent rise in global yields.

Recapping last week now, and as mentioned at the top, the biggest story was the selloff in AI-related assets, with chip stocks taking a particular hit. For instance, the Philly semiconductor index was down -11.41% last week (-3.83% Friday), whilst the NASDAQ was down -4.48% (-2.14% Friday). Moreover, there were even larger declines for some of the most affected names, with CoreWeave down -25.21% last week (-11.91% Friday), whilst CoreWeave’s 5yr CDS was up +225bps on the week to 1128bps. Meanwhile, Oracle’s share price was down -9.31% (-4.64% Friday), and their 5yr CDS was up +44bps to 300bps. So given the weighting of tech in US equities more broadly, that meant the S&P 500 took a hit as well, with the index down -1.94% last week (-1.09% Friday). However, that selloff in the AI space didn’t carry over to other sectors in general, with the equal-weighted S&P 500 posting a weekly gain of +0.50% (-0.40% Friday). Moreover, European equities actually posted solid gains, with the STOXX 600 up +2.13% (+0.72% Friday), marking its best weekly performance since July. That said, some indices more exposed to chip stocks struggled, and Japan’s Nikkei fell -5.37% (+1.39% Friday), marking its worst week since July.

As all that was happening, AI-related growth concerns helped to drive a decent rally for sovereign bonds, with the US 10yr Treasury yield down -16.5bps last week (+1.5bps Friday) to 5.07%. Indeed, it was the biggest weekly decline for the 10yr yield since August 2025, whilst the 30yr Treasury yield fell -17.5bps (+1.5bps Friday) in its biggest weekly decline since April 2025. Interestingly, that came despite some very hawkish data last week, as the US core CPI print was at +0.3% in September, which briefly saw futures price in a greater-than-50% chance of a hike at the Fed’s October meeting. However, the AI selloff then meant that quickly unwound, and Fed Chair Warsh’s comments at the end of the week saw market pricing for an October Fed hike at 17% by the close on Friday.

Staying on rates, last week saw the stress around French bonds continue to stabilise. Indeed, the 2yr Franco-German spread came down another -4.5bps to 47bps, whilst the 10yr spread was broadly steady, up just +0.5bps at 137bps. We’ll see what the weekend riots do to sentiment this morning. That came alongside a wider decline in sovereign bond yields across the continent, with 10yr bund yields down -5.5bps (+1.3bps Friday) to 3.42%. Nevertheless, there was more stress in HY credit, with Euro HY spreads up +12bps last week, and US HY up +24bps as well. However, IG spreads were more contained, with Euro IG down -2bps, and US IG up +3bps.

Finally, the risk-off tone wasn’t helped by the continued rise in oil prices, with Brent crude up +4.91% last week (+3.72% Friday) to $109.86/bbl. That marks a second consecutive weekly increase, and it also came alongside fresh gains for European natural gas futures, which moved up +7.51% last week to their highest level since 2022, at €87.55/MWh. So that exacerbated inflation concerns in Europe and saw the 1yr Euro inflation swap rise another +21bps last week to +3.69%. And similarly in the US, the 1yr inflation swap was up +17bps last week to +2.74%.
